newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX crude oil ends sharply higher on Iraq news.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX crude oil ends sharply higher on Iraq news.

text.p: NYMEX crude oil prices ended sharply higher, as did refined products, on news that the United Nations suspended the Iraqi oil-for-food exchange, but some traders said crude's price was now overextended.
October crude closed up $1.15 to $23.40 a barrel, after reaching a contract high of $24.25 during the day.
"Most of the value gained today was ultimately from the fact we will not see 700,000 barrels a day of oil from the deal any time soon," a trader said.
However, the trader said 700,000 barrels was not enough supply being removed to merit Tuesday's rise in crude's price.
The United Nations would have permitted Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil in exchange for food and huminatrian aid.
The 700,000 barrels per day estimated from the deal is equivalent to less than a tenth of U.S. oil imports daily.

"I would expect to see some consolidation tomorrow" a trader said. He said crude prices gapped higher in the open and on Wednesday will likely test the gap which starts at $22.85 a barrel and extends down to $22.25.
Meanhwile, October heating oil, following crude's move, closed up 1.95 cents to 65.07 cents a gallon, and October gasoline settled up 1.35 cents a gallon to 62.96 cents.
Military incursions by Iraq into its northern Kurdish regions over the weekend led the United Nations to suspend the oil-for-food deal.
The United States responded to Iraq's actions by launching a missile attack on southern Iraq.
Traders said prices traded more on the suspension of the oil-for-food exchange than the U.S. missile attack, but they said heightened hostility in the Middle East could add to price volatility.
"The military issue is a long term issue, but the oil-for-food deal clearly outwieghs it," said Rita Beale, an analyst with Fimat USA Futures.
Beale said the 700,000 barrels would have been easily absorbed by the market given the historically low inventories of heating oil.
The low stocks have made crude supply an issue since high refinery runs will be required to meet heating oil demand in the winter.
However, Beale expected crude's prices to consolidate tomorrow.
"I think the front month may have gotten a little overextended," said Beale of October crude's price rise.
-- Harry Milling, New York Energy Desk, +1 212-859-1761
